Crypto currency in games

Project 32 · a report · written September 2026 · index

Summary. Putting a cryptocurrency inside a game turns the game into a small central bank with players as its currency market. Every well-known attempt since 2017 has hit the same three walls: a token that only has value while new players arrive, a platform that will not carry it, and a player base that experiences the wallet as a tax on fun. The cases where it worked are the ones where the crypto part was invisible, optional, or both. For this repo’s 31 idle games the recommendation is plain: keep the counters local, and if a shared currency is ever wanted, use the ship’s own HEZE ledger, which is a unit of account with an issuer, not a speculative token.

1. What “crypto in a game” has actually meant

Collectible on-chain items (2017–)

CryptoKitties, Gods Unchained, Sorare. The token is the item: a cat, a card, a footballer. The chain is a title registry. The game logic mostly stays off-chain.

Play-to-earn (2020–2022)

Axie Infinity and its imitators. A soft token is minted by play and burned by breeding or upgrading. Players in the Philippines and Venezuela earned wages from it at the peak. It is the model that produced the biggest gains and the biggest losses.

Virtual land and metaverse (2021–)

The Sandbox, Decentraland. Parcels as NFTs, a governance token, a promise of foot traffic that mostly did not arrive. Land sold in the tens of thousands of dollars now trades for a fraction.

Move-to-earn and app tokens (2022)

STEPN. Buy shoe NFTs, walk, earn a token, sell the token. A textbook inflow-dependent loop; the token fell over ninety percent within months of its peak.

Invisible chains (2023–)

Studios that keep an on-chain registry for provenance but hide wallets, gas and tokens behind ordinary accounts. This is the survivable form. Players do not notice, which is the point.

Casino and prediction games

Dice, crash, coin-flip sites on-chain. Not games in the sense this repo means; they are gambling with a smart contract as the house. Regulated as such almost everywhere.

2. The economics, in one paragraph and one table

A game token is a currency whose only sink is the game’s own design and whose only source of outside value is new buyers. If earning is easy and sinks are weak, the token inflates; if the studio then tightens sinks, early players who were promised income revolt. Axie’s Smooth Love Potion is the clean case: it was minted per match, burned only by breeding, and once breeding demand stalled it fell from about 35 cents to under a cent. The cheapest honest description is that a play-to-earn token is a wage paid in shares of the studio’s future growth, and the players are the last shareholders in.

3. The three walls

The platform wall

Valve banned blockchain and NFT games from Steam in October 2021 and has not reversed it. Apple and Google allow NFT purchases only through their own in-app billing, which takes thirty percent and forbids using the NFT to unlock features bought elsewhere. Epic allows blockchain games on its store, with warnings. Console makers publish nothing and approve nothing. A crypto game therefore ships mostly on the web or on its own launcher, which halves its reachable audience before it starts.

The regulatory wall

A token that is bought expecting profit from the studio’s work is a security under the Howey test in the United States, and studios have been careful to call theirs “utility” tokens for exactly that reason. Loot boxes are already gambling in Belgium and the Netherlands; a randomised NFT drop with a resale market is a stronger case than a loot box. Know-your-customer rules apply the moment a token is cashed out. None of this is settled law, which is worse for a studio than settled law would be.

The player wall

The Ubisoft Quartz trailer was among the most disliked videos the company ever posted. The GSC Game World (Stalker 2) NFT plan was withdrawn within a day of announcement. Players read a wallet as a sign that the studio’s incentive has moved from making the game good to making the token go up, and they are usually right. The studios that survived did not argue with this; they hid the chain.

4. Where it genuinely helps

  • Provenance of rare items across a studio’s own titles, when the studio wants a public registry it cannot quietly edit.
  • Player-run economies with real withdrawal, where the game is honest that it is a market (EVE Online is the non-crypto ancestor; its PLEX is a company-issued unit, not a token, and it has worked for twenty years).
  • Interoperable items between independent games in one shared universe, if and only if the games agree on a schema first. This is rarer than the pitch decks say.
  • Auditability of drop rates, since a verifiable random function on-chain is a stronger promise than a published percentage.

5. Design rules, if you do it anyway

  1. Sinks before sources. Decide what destroys the token before deciding what mints it.
  2. One unit, one issuer, published issuance. A fixed-or-scheduled supply that players can recompute, not a treasury that “manages” it.
  3. No promise of income. The moment earnings are the pitch, the game is a job with a variable wage.
  4. Custody is your problem. Players will lose keys; if the answer is “that is the point of crypto”, the game is for a hundred people.
  5. Bridges are the attack surface. Ronin lost six hundred and twenty million dollars through five of nine validator keys. If history must cross ledgers, recompute both sides (see project 34).
  6. Make it optional. The player who never opens a wallet must get the entire game.

6. This repo

The thirty-one idle games under idle/ keep a counter and a worker count in the browser’s localStorage, keyed per game. Nothing transfers, nothing is scarce, nothing is owned, and that is the correct design for a clicker. The ship already has a ledger, HEZE, with doors, tranches, a unit of account and six-monthly syndication with recomputable checkpoints; it was built as a lesson in fungibility and decentralization rather than as a token, and it has an issuer that stands behind it. If the idle games ever need a shared currency, the right move is to let them draw on a HEZE door like any other syndicate, with the games as sinks and the doors as the only source. The wrong move is a new token.

Recommendation. Do not add a cryptocurrency to the games. If a common currency is wanted, issue it from HEZE, make the games pure sinks, and publish the issuance schedule on the page where the counter lives.
